docs.title: Fall 2026 · HKUST-GZ
docs.text:
Welcome to DSAA3073 - Theories in Data Science!

This course provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for data science, covering statistical learning theory, classical methods, ensemble learning, and online learning algorithms.

docs.title: 🎯 Course Overview
docs.text: This course is organized into five Parts across ten teaching weeks, followed by three student-presentation weeks.

docs.title: Course Structure (13 Weeks, 5 Parts)
docs.text:
Part 1: Mathematical Preliminaries (Weeks 1–2)

  • Probability, concentration inequalities, norms, and Hilbert spaces
  • Convexity, optimization, and computational complexity

Part 2: PAC Learning Framework (Weeks 3–4)

  • Risk, ERM, PAC learning, finite hypothesis classes, and VC dimension
  • Agnostic PAC learning, uniform convergence, Rademacher complexity, and symmetrization

Part 3: Classical Methods (Weeks 5–6)

  • Bias–variance, ill-posed problems, Tikhonov regularization, and ridge regression
  • Cross-validation, LOOCV, PRESS, AIC, BIC, and honest model selection

Part 4: Ensemble Learning (Weeks 7–8)

  • Weak learning, AdaBoost, and training-error guarantees
  • Margins, exponential loss, and coordinate-descent interpretations

Part 5: Online Learning (Weeks 9–10)

  • Expert advice, Halving, Weighted Majority, and multiplicative weights
  • Online convex optimization, OGD, FTL, FTRL, and online-to-batch conversion

Student Presentations (Weeks 11–13)

  • Each presentation is based on an individually completed, instructor-approved written assignment or programming project.
  • Detailed presentation requirements and student order: TBD
  • Student presentations contribute 30% of the course grade.

docs.title: Weekly Format
docs.text:
• A comprehensive Learning Sheet for each teaching week in Weeks 1–10
  • A weekly Validation Sheet for checking understanding
  • A concise Cheatsheet for each content week in Weeks 1–10
  • Weekly Open Investigations for research-oriented exploration
  • Five equally weighted 30-minute, 120-mark Part Tests, each containing four multiple-choice questions and six short-answer questions, together worth 70%
  • A 50-minute Tuesday Tutorial for collaborative learning and support
  • Student presentations in Weeks 11–13, worth 30%

docs.title: How to Succeed
docs.text:
1. Work through each Learning Sheet in sequence.
  2. Use the weekly Validation Sheet to check your understanding.
  3. Work through the Open Investigation after completing the core material.
  4. Review both weeks in a Part before its Test.
  5. Ask questions during class and attend the Tuesday Tutorial.

docs.title: 🎓 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  1. Use the mathematical tools required for learning-theory arguments.
  2. Analyze generalization guarantees and sample complexity.
  3. Apply PAC, VC, uniform-convergence, and complexity-based frameworks.
  4. Analyze regularization and model-selection methods.
  5. Derive guarantees for boosting and online-learning algorithms.
  6. Communicate a theoretical data-science topic in a student presentation.

docs.title: 💡 Prerequisites
docs.text:
This course assumes:

  • ✅ Strong foundations in linear algebra, calculus, and probability
  • ✅ Familiarity with basic algorithms and data structures
  • ✅ Comfort with mathematical proofs and formal reasoning
  • ✅ Programming experience for implementing theoretical concepts

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
You are free to choose a written assignment or a programming project for this course. The assignment/project should be closely related to the topics covered in the course. You must obtain approval from the instructor before starting your work. The assignment/project should be completed individually, and you are expected to submit your work by the middle of the examination period of this semester.

Your student presentation in Weeks 11–13 will be based on this approved assignment or programming project. Together, the project work and its presentation contribute 30% of the course grade.

Some ideas for the assignment/project include:

  • Implementing a specific algorithm or data structure discussed in the course, then analyzing its performance and possible improvements.
  • Conducting a small research project on a topic related to the course, such as exploring a new problem from a theoretical aspect (for example, a model or a hypothesis).
  • Possible topics:
    • Investigate how an LLM generalizes in the OOD case.
    • Explore alternative theoretical models to explain the generalization and PEFT of foundation models.
    • Explore Grokking and its theoretical foundations.

docs.title: Grade Descriptors
docs.text: Grade Performance Level Description A Excellent Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of learning theory and can construct rigorous proofs, apply guarantees fluently, and synthesize concepts across Parts. B Good Shows solid understanding of core concepts and correctly applies techniques to most problems, with only minor gaps. C Satisfactory Demonstrates adequate knowledge of fundamental definitions and theorems and can solve routine problems. D Marginal Pass Shows threshold understanding of basic concepts but has difficulty with proofs and theoretical analysis. F Fail Demonstrates insufficient understanding of core concepts and does not meet minimum requirements.

  5. Instructor and TA support during scheduled class and Tutorial time.
